extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Recognizing and characterizing common a priori fallacies and natural prejudices that mislead philosophical and scientific inquiry; used to evaluate reasoning, experimental claims, and methodological assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The misapprehension that general language or abstract ideas denote outward objective realities — i.e., ascribing objective existence to subjective creations of the mind (universals treated as real distinct entities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as treating names of qualities and substances as standing for the same external facts and then elevating abstract/general terms (e.g., 'man' in general, 'being') to the status of unique, immutable subjects of science. Examples include believing in Universal Substances or τὸ ὄν, and the historical tendency (Vedas, Platonists, Hegelians) to consider mental ideas as objects whose contemplation yields knowledge of the world. The passage labels this whole error 'Mysticism' and warns it ends intelligible discussion by substituting inward creations for empirical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing nature as under incapacities corresponding to those of our intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because we cannot conceive something, nature therefore cannot do it (treating human conceivability as a constraint on what is possible in nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes using our cognitive limitations as grounds for claims about nature. It situates this error adjacent to other a priori fallacies and warns that it underlies many unjustified a priori conclusions; it can be reframed as a petitio principii when hidden premises about conceivability are smuggled into arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of the Sufficient Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring that a phenomenon must follow a particular law because we see no reason why it should deviate (i.e., asserting laws a priori from absence of an apparent alternative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage criticizes using the Principle of the Sufficient Reason to 'prove' physical laws without experience. Detailed examples: attempted a priori proofs of the law of inertia and the first law of motion that argue a body cannot begin or change motion because 'there is no reason' it should go one way rather than another. Mill (via examples) shows this reasoning is fallacious — internal impulses or unknown natural laws could account for motion — and concludes the only real proof of physical laws is experience, not the absence-of-reason arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming the same distinctions in nature as in our received language (language-prejudice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Believing that effects or objects which ordinary language separates must correspond to distinct natures or causes in nature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as the early-stage scientific prejudice that classes made by popular phrases are natural classes. Examples and authorities (Aristotle, Thales, Whewell) are cited: philosophers deriving philosophical dogmas by analyzing common language (e.g., the many senses of 'in', using words to infer facts like the inexistence of void). The guidance warns that elevating linguistic distinctions above empirical investigation makes truth depend on word usage rather than facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Contrarieties (inferring natural oppositions from linguistic or conceptual opposites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that adjectives or concepts that are opposites in language or thought (e.g., Right/Left, Rest/Motion) must point to fundamental antitheses in nature worthy of scientific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text exemplifies this mode by citing the Pythagoreans and Aristotle, who derived cosmological or physical dogmas (e.g., four elements) from such oppositions. The guidance is to be wary of inferring ontological dualities simply from contrasts present in language or abstract thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming a single, uniform cause (Bacon's oversight: neglect of plurality of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating a phenomenon as having one invariable 'forma' or cause present in all instances, rather than accepting that phenomena often arise from multiple, varied causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill criticizes Bacon for tacitly assuming phenomena have one cause, especially problematic for sensible qualities (color, taste, etc.), where no unity of cause is found. The guidance is methodological: inquiries should allow for plurality of causes and focus more fruitfully on 'effects of a given cause' (which experiment can probe) than on attempting to deduce one cause of a given effect by elimination alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The prejudice that the conditions of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that causes or conditions of an effect must resemble the effect itself ('like produces like').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage documents many manifestations: contagion, imitation, doctrine of signatures (using resemblance to pick remedies), ancient attempts to infer compound properties from element properties, Cartesian insistence that motion must be caused by motion, planetary attributions (Mars->war), and various metaphysical theories (species sensibiles, ideas-as-images). The guidance: resemblance between cause and effect is sometimes true but is a weak heuristic and often misleading; it should not be taken as a general principle for inferring causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing conditions/cause with the phenomenon (treating the condition as the very thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to distinguish between an effect and the conditions or causes of that effect, and therefore identifying the condition with the phenomenon itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Bacon's language (saying heat 'is' a kind of motion when he meant its conditions) and Darwin's Zoonomia (defining 'idea' as a configuration/motion of fibres). The passage warns this verbal confusion leads to conceptual errors — writers may speak as if conditions and effects are identical, obscuring whether one is discussing the mental phenomenon or its physiological/physical correlates. Methodological guidance: maintain clear conceptual distinctions between phenomenon and its causal conditions.
